title: Pipeline Overview - Microsoft Fabric
summary: Introduces the pipeline as the orchestration unit in Fabric Data Factory: a logical grouping of activities that is deployed, scheduled, and monitored as a set rather than individually. Covers the three activity categories, the three ways a pipeline run can be started, the role of parameters versus variables, and the monitoring surfaces available once a pipeline is running.
audience: Data engineers and architects deciding how to structure orchestration logic in Fabric before drilling into individual activity types.
why_it_matters: This is the conceptual entry point for metadata-driven design: it frames pipelines as reusable units driven by parameters and triggers rather than bespoke one-off jobs, which is the premise a control-table-driven ingestion pattern builds on.
takeaways: A pipeline groups activities so they can be deployed and scheduled as a single unit instead of managed individually.
Activities fall into three categories — data movement, data transformation, and control flow — and can be chained based on success, failure, or completion of the prior activity.
Pipelines can be started on-demand, on a schedule, or by an event trigger (such as a new file landing), which is what allows a metadata-driven pipeline to react to external conditions.
Parameters make a pipeline reusable across different configurations, while variables hold transient state during a single run.
Recommended practice is to parameterize connections and file paths specifically, which is the direct mechanism for building one pipeline that serves many sources.

claims.text: A pipeline in Fabric Data Factory is a logical grouping of activities that is deployed and scheduled as one unit, rather than requiring each activity to be managed independently.

Pipeline activities fall into three categories: data movement activities that copy data between sources and destinations, data transformation activities that clean and reshape data, and control flow activities that add conditions, loops, and error handling.

Activities can be chained so that completion of one triggers the next based on the prior activity's outcome — success, failure, or completion — enabling branching error-handling logic within a single pipeline.
Every pipeline run is assigned its own unique run ID used for tracking and monitoring that specific execution.

A Fabric pipeline can be started three ways: an on-demand manual run from the editor, a scheduled run with configured start/end dates, frequency, and time zone, or an event-based trigger that fires on conditions such as a new file arriving in a data lake or a database change.
Parameters let the same pipeline process different datasets or configurations across runs, while variables are used to hold temporary values or pass data between activities within a single run.

Fabric's documented pipeline monitoring surfaces include real-time run progress with per-activity status indicators, run history for troubleshooting, performance metrics for execution time and resource usage, and an audit trail of who ran what and when.

Recommended pipeline design practice includes starting with simple data movement before adding complexity, and specifically parameterizing connections and file paths to keep pipelines reusable rather than hard-coded.
